opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more important questions, and I'm cautiously optimistic, though for somewhat different reasons than people sometimes expect.

The basic picture is this. If interpretability is going to matter for the systems we actually care about, the ones big and capable enough to be risky, it can't be a project where humans stare at individual neurons and write up what each circuit does. There's far too much going on in these models. Even if you could understand a small fraction of a frontier model by hand, that fraction probably isn't where the interesting, dangerous cognition lives. So almost by necessity, the version of interpretability that pays off at scale is mostly automated. Humans set up the framework and check the methodology, and AI systems do most of the actual explaining.

The hard part is less "can a model generate plausible explanations of what a neuron or feature does." We've seen that it sort of can, at least for simple features. The hard part is knowing whether those explanations are actually *true*, and true in the sense that matters. You want explanations that capture why the model behaves the way it does, so that if it's doing something weird on some input, like reasoning about whether it's being tested, the explanation would reveal that. A pile of locally plausible labels doesn't get you there. You need some notion of what makes an explanation good, something like "this explanation accounts for the model's behavior, and anything it leaves out really is noise." Making that precise is a big part of what I've been working on, under the heading of heuristic arguments or formalizing explanations.

So I'd split it into two problems. One is the definitional or theoretical problem: what are we even searching for when we search for an explanation, and how would we recognize a good one? The other is the search problem: given that definition, can you find good explanations efficiently, ideally by having ML do the search, the same way we found the model in the first place with gradient descent? My hope is that if you nail the first problem well enough, the second starts to look like a normal ML problem, and you can leverage the same scaling that produced the capabilities. That's the optimistic case: interpretability keeps pace with the model because it's powered by the same kind of optimization.

The pessimistic case is that explanations of what a large model is doing are just intrinsically much harder to find than the model itself, that there's an asymmetry where gradient descent can stumble into some messy but effective computation and there's no comparably cheap way to produce an account of it. I don't think we know that's false. But I don't see a strong reason to believe it either, and there are some reasons for hope. Whenever gradient descent finds a structure, there's in some sense a reason it worked, some regularity in the data it's exploiting, and you'd like to argue that the explanation can piggyback on that same process.

There's also a nearer-term, more practical version that I think is clearly worth doing: using current models to help with the grunt work of interpretability, proposing hypotheses, running ablations, summarizing features, and treating that as tooling for human researchers. That will help a lot and is already helping. I just don't think it's the whole story. The real question for safety is whether you get to the point where you can ask "why did the model do this?" and get an answer you can trust even when the model might be actively optimizing against you. That requires both the automation and a much clearer sense of what an explanation is supposed to guarantee.

If I had to put a number on it, I'd say there's a meaningful chance, maybe something like a coin flip or a bit worse, that some version of automated interpretability ends up being a significant part of how we handle risks from very capable systems. And even in the worlds where it falls short of that, I think the attempt teaches us a lot about what's going on inside these models, which is valuable on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could automate much of interpretability and help with specific tasks, but it does not propose training systems to perform the tasks humans do in existing interpretability workflows.

r002.rationale: It says human inspection cannot cover enough of a frontier model, but does not identify whether the model decomposes into human-sized pieces as a condition for automation by imitating human work.

r003.rationale: The response is optimistic that ML could search for explanations, but does not say that a method can be automated even if it is extremely labor-intensive for humans.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the more promising directions, and also one where I'd want to be careful about what exactly we mean by "automating."

The optimistic case goes something like this. Interpretability right now is enormously labor-intensive. A small number of researchers spend weeks or months understanding a handful of circuits in a model with hundreds of billions of parameters. That obviously doesn't scale. But the kind of work they're doing, forming hypotheses about what a component does, designing probes or ablations to test it, looking at activations across many inputs, writing up the finding, is the kind of thing that looks increasingly amenable to being done by AI systems themselves. So you could imagine a world where you point a model at another model, or at itself, and it generates and tests thousands of hypotheses in parallel. That could change interpretability from a craft into something more like an industrial process.

And I think the structural reason to be hopeful is that a lot of interpretability has a checkable flavor. If a model claims "this neuron fires on references to the Golden Gate Bridge," you can go verify that empirically. If it claims "this circuit implements modular addition," you can ablate it and see if performance on modular addition collapses. So the task has a feedback loop that doesn't depend entirely on trusting the model doing the interpreting, which is exactly the property you want when you're using AI to oversee AI.

That said, there are a few things I'd worry about.

The first is that the easy-to-verify claims may not be the ones that matter. Finding feature detectors is nice, but the questions we actually care about for safety are more like, "Is this model being deceptive?" or "What is it actually optimizing for in this situation?" Those are much harder to turn into a crisp test. And an automated interpretability pipeline is going to be pulled toward whatever it can get a clean signal on, which may mean we generate enormous volumes of true-but-unimportant explanations while the hard questions go unanswered.

The second worry is about the explainer itself. If the model doing the interpreting is roughly as capable as the model being interpreted, and especially if it's the same model, then you've got an obvious problem: a system that wanted to hide something from you is in a decent position to produce plausible-sounding explanations that are subtly wrong. You'd need the verification step to be robust against an adversarial explainer, not just an honest-but-mistaken one. I don't think that's hopeless, that's sort of the whole game in a lot of my work on scalable oversight, but it's a real constraint on how much you can lean on this.

And the third thing is more mundane: I think there's a risk we fool ourselves about what "understanding" means. If an automated system produces a million natural-language descriptions of features and they all pass some automated scoring metric, that feels like progress. But the question is whether a human, or a human plus tools, can use that to actually predict what the model will do in a new situation, or to catch something going wrong. It's easy to optimize the metric and lose the thing.

So my overall view is that automation is probably necessary. I don't see a path where humans alone interpret frontier models in enough detail to matter. But I'd think of it less as "automating interpretability" and more as "building a system where AI does the bulk of the work and humans retain the ability to check it." The crucial research questions are about where the trust bottoms out: what are the claims that are cheap to verify and hard to fake, and can you build the whole edifice on top of those?

If that works, I think it's one of the better bets we have. If it turns out the interesting properties of models just aren't decomposable in a way that admits that kind of verification, then I'd be considerably more pessimistic, and we'd be relying more heavily on behavioral methods, which I find less reassuring.

r001.rationale: The response proposes having AI systems generate and test interpretability hypotheses, but does not say to train them to perform the tasks in existing human workflows.

r002.rationale: The response says interpretability could fail if model properties are not decomposable in a verifiable way, but does not identify decomposition into human-sized pieces as a condition for automation.

r003.rationale: It explicitly calls interpretability labor-intensive for humans, then presents an optimistic case that AI could perform that work at scale.

astra-6.text:
I’m fairly optimistic that a lot of interpretability research can be automated. You’re looking at a complicated object, proposing hypotheses about what’s happening inside it, and running experiments to distinguish those hypotheses. Those are all things I expect AI systems to get substantially better at.

The question I’m more uncertain about is what kind of understanding we’ll get, and whether it will be enough to answer the questions we care about for safety. Understanding why a model produces a particular answer is different from being able to say, “This model won’t deliberately undermine our oversight in some situation we haven’t tested.” Automating the research doesn’t automatically close that gap.

There’s also an interesting issue if the system doing the interpretability work is itself one you don’t fully trust. Suppose it tells you, “I looked inside this other model, and everything seems fine.” That’s not very reassuring by itself. You’d like it to produce explanations and experimental predictions that you can check, so that you don’t have to trust its judgment about the conclusion.

So I think the promising picture is AI doing a huge amount of the work of generating hypotheses, designing experiments, and finding mechanisms, with humans checking a much smaller amount of evidence. The uncertainty is whether the evidence can actually be made compact and convincing enough. I’m optimistic about accelerating the science; I’m less confident that the resulting science will give us the assurances we ultimately want.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems can take on interpretability work humans do, including generating hypotheses, designing experiments, and finding mechanisms. That communicates automating the workflow through AI systems.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether large models can be decomposed into human-sized pieces.

r003.rationale: The response is optimistic about automating interpretability research, but does not say automation remains viable even when the method is extremely labor-intensive for humans.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m pretty optimistic that we can automate a lot of the work involved in interpretability. If a human can look at a collection of examples, form a hypothesis about what some part of a model is doing, and design experiments to test that hypothesis, those seem like activities that AI systems could help with substantially.

The harder question is what you want to get out of that process. There’s a big difference between generating a plausible explanation of a model’s behavior and giving us reliable evidence that the model isn’t doing something dangerous. You could automate the production of explanations and still have a hard time telling whether those explanations are faithful or whether you’ve missed something important.

So I’d be excited about a setup where AI systems propose explanations and experiments, and we check their predictions by intervening on the model. You want the explanation to let you predict what happens when you change something, including in cases you haven’t already examined. That gives you a way to make progress beyond judging whether a story sounds convincing.

There’s also a trust issue if you’re relying on a potentially untrustworthy AI to explain another potentially untrustworthy AI. That doesn’t make the approach hopeless, but you need some reason to believe that a misleading explanation would get caught. Automating interpretability could make investigation dramatically cheaper. Whether that translates into strong safety guarantees depends on how good our checks are and what kinds of failures we’re trying to rule out.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems could help with human interpretability activities and propose explanations and experiments, but does not clearly propose training ML systems to perform those workflow tasks.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss whether large models decompose into pieces small enough for humans to understand.

r003.rationale: It is optimistic about automating interpretability, but does not state that a method that works can be automated even when it is extremely labor-intensive for humans.
